mainEntity.name: How much does a Mercedes Sprinter 209-319 CDI engine replacement cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: A rebuilt OM646 engine for the Sprinter 209 CDI costs £2,600-£3,600 supply-only; a rebuilt OM642 V6 engine for the Sprinter 319 CDI costs £4,200-£6,000 supply-only. Supply-and-fit adds £450-£850 labour depending on complexity - V6 work requires specialist knowledge.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of injector seal failure on a Mercedes Sprinter 209 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Diesel fumes in the cabin and carbon buildup around the injectors are the classic warning signs on the OM646 engine. The copper sealing washers fail over time, allowing combustion gases to escape ('Black Death'). If ignored, injectors can seize in the head.

mainEntity.name: What are the signs of oil cooler seal failure on a Mercedes Sprinter 319 CDI (OM642)?

acceptedAnswer.text: A burning oil smell from the engine bay or oil pooling in the V of the engine is the classic warning sign on the OM642 V6. The seals are located under the intake manifold and require significant labour to replace.

mainEntity.name: Is the Mercedes Sprinter 319 CDI V6 engine (OM642) reliable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The OM642 V6 is a fundamentally strong and refined engine, found across Mercedes' commercial and passenger vehicle ranges. However, it has well-documented weak points: oil cooler seal degradation, turbocharger oil seal failure, and injector cup leaks. With upgraded Viton seals and regular maintenance, these engines routinely exceed 150,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: How long do Mercedes Sprinter 209-319 CDI engines last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Properly maintained OM646 engines routinely reach 150,000-200,000 miles before major work. The OM642 V6 can achieve similar mileage but may require oil cooler seal attention between 80,000-130,000 miles.

mainEntity.name: Is it worth replacing the engine in my Mercedes Sprinter 209-319 CDI?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, if the Sprinter is otherwise in good condition with no structural rust or major transmission faults. A rebuilt OM646 costs £2,600-£3,600 - far less than replacing a £3,000-£8,000 vehicle. The OM642's higher value (£5,000-£15,000) makes replacement even more financially justifiable.

historyTimeline.h2: Mercedes Benz Sprinter 209/219/309/319 CDI - Engine History & Specs at a Glance
historyTimeline.intro: The W906 Sprinter launched in 2006 with the OM646 2.1-litre four-cylinder diesel powering entry-level 209/309 CDI variants, while the OM642 3.0-litre V6 diesel was introduced in 2009 for heavy-duty 319 CDI applications. The 209 CDI produced 88hp (65kW) from the OM646.984 engine, while the 319 CDI delivered 190hp (140kW) from the OM642.896 V6. These engines represented the entry-level and premium diesel options in the Sprinter range, with the OM642 V6 reserved for high-payload, towing, and passenger shuttle applications requiring superior mid-range torque. Production continued through to 2018 when the VS30 generation introduced the OM654 engine and updated OM642 variants.

milestones.description: OM646.984, 2.1L four-cylinder diesel, 88hp (209 CDI, 309 CDI, W906 launch)
OM642.896, 3.0L V6 diesel, 190hp (319 CDI, W906 V6 introduction)

commonProblems.h2: Mercedes Sprinter 209/219/309/319 CDI Engine Problems - Repair Cost vs Replacement
commonProblems.h3: The Sprinter 209 CDI's OM646 four-cylinder and the 319 CDI's OM642 V6 diesel are two very different engines - the OM646 is a robust entry-level workhorse, while the OM642 is a refined, torquey V6 designed for heavy-duty applications. However, both have well-documented weaknesses that can lead to significant repair costs. The OM646 suffers from injector seal leakage (Black Death), crankshaft sensor failure, and turbo actuator issues, while the OM642 is prone to oil cooler seal degradation, turbocharger oil seal failure, and injector cup leaks. Every rebuilt engine supplied through EnginesMarket includes upgraded components addressing these original failure points, plus a minimum 12-month unlimited-mileage warranty.

problems.h4: OM646 Injector Seal Failure (Black Death) - The 209 CDI's Most Common Weakness
problems.rootCause: Copper injector seals fail over time, allowing high-pressure combustion gases to blow past the injector. The leaking gases bake into a hard, tar-like carbon crust around the injector - "Black Death". Left long enough, the injector becomes welded into the head. Carbon buildup leads to compression loss, rough running, and eventual cylinder head damage.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace copper sealing washer, clean injector bore, leak-off test
repairOptions.longevity: Effective if caught early before injector seizes

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Replace all four copper sealing washers, clean injector bores, new hold-down bolts
repairOptions.longevity: If multiple injectors are leaking or preventative maintenance

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Specialty pullers, head work, injector seat machining
repairOptions.longevity: If injector has seized and requires extraction

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Supply & fit rebuilt OM646 with new injectors and seals, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: If injector damage has caused cylinder or head damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2006-2009 Sprinter 209/309 CDI is worth approximately £3,000-£8,000 depending on condition and mileage. A rebuilt OM646 engine costing £2,600-£3,600 typically extends vehicle life by 80,000-120,000 miles, making replacement significantly more economical than purchasing a new or used replacement van.
problems.recommendation: Injector seal leaks on the OM646 are common but manageable. If you notice diesel fumes in the cabin or see carbon buildup around the injectors, have a specialist inspect the seals immediately. Caught early, resealing an injector is a £150-£250 job. Caught late, extracting a seized injector can require specialty pullers and head work. On a commercial Sprinter worth £3,000-£8,000, preventative injector seal replacement is always the better investment.

problems.h4: OM642 Oil Cooler Seal Degradation - The 319 CDI V6's Most Expensive Leak
problems.affectedModels: Mercedes Sprinter 319 CDI, 419 CDI, 519 CDI (OM642.896, OM642.898, 2009-2018)
problems.rootCause: The OM642's oil cooler is located in the V of the engine, under the intake manifold. The factory seals degrade under heat cycling, allowing oil to leak into the valley. This is a labour-intensive repair requiring removal of the intake manifold, turbocharger, and associated components. If ignored, oil loss can lead to bearing failure and engine seizure.

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Remove intake manifold, turbo, replace oil cooler seals with upgraded Viton units, clean valley, reassemble
repairOptions.longevity: If caught early with no other damage; upgraded seals prevent recurrence

repairOptions.tier: Major - Oil cooler & EGR service (while open)
repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Oil cooler seals, EGR cooler cleaning, swirl flap inspection, intake decarbonisation
repairOptions.longevity: Best performed while intake is off - saves duplicate labour

repairOptions.whatItInvolves: Complete V6 swap with upgraded seals, new gaskets, bench-tested, 12-month warranty
repairOptions.longevity: If oil loss has caused bearing or bottom-end damage

problems.vehicleValueCheck: A typical 2009-2018 Sprinter 319 CDI is worth approximately £5,000-£15,000 depending on generation, mileage and condition. The OM642's complexity means repair costs can approach replacement costs - for high-mileage examples with multiple issues, a full rebuilt engine is often the more economical choice.
problems.recommendation: The OM642 oil leak is progressive. If caught early - oil pooling in the valley or a burning oil smell - the specialist seal overhaul at £1,200-£1,800 extends engine life affordably. Once coolant has entered the oil or bearing damage has occurred, patch repairs are futile. For high-mileage 319 CDI models, a rebuilt OM642 with upgraded Viton seals delivers superior long-term value and peace of mind.
